lessons.title: Detecting Distributional Shift and Out-of-Distribution States

body.text: An agent operating in a state it never trained on does not know it is out of its depth. It keeps acting with the same confidence it had on familiar ground. This lesson builds the tools that catch what the agent itself cannot: distribution comparisons for batches of data, and a real-time check for individual live states.

children.text: Recap: Why Distributional Shift Is the Quiet Killer

Chapter 1 named distributional shift as the reason an agent can perform well for weeks and then fail without any bug in the code: live conditions have simply drifted into territory its training data never covered. Chapter 3's POMDP discussion and Chapter 4's training-time non-stationarity table both returned to versions of the same idea. This lesson stops describing the problem and builds two concrete tools for catching it.
Comparing Feature Distributions: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test

The simplest starting point compares the distribution of each state feature in the training data against a batch of newer data, live or a recent validation window, one feature at a time. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test does exactly this, producing a statistic measuring how far apart two empirical distributions are, and a p-value for how likely a gap that large is to occur by chance if the two samples actually came from the same distribution.

body.caption: alpha=0.01 sets how strict the test is: a p-value below alpha means the two samples are unlikely to come from the same distribution purely by chance, and the feature gets flagged as shifted.
Verified Output: Only the Deliberately Shifted Feature Gets Flagged

children.text: This test was run against a live sample deliberately built with india_vix shifted to a higher mean and wider spread, a stand-in for a genuinely more volatile regime, while the other three features were left unchanged. The KS test correctly flagged only india_vix and correctly left the other three alone, exactly the selective behavior a useful monitoring tool needs: not every feature drifting a little, but the one that actually changed.
Population Stability Index: A Single Number, With Standard Thresholds

The Population Stability Index (PSI), a standard tool from credit risk and general model monitoring, offers a complementary single number per feature rather than a statistical test. It bins the reference (training) distribution into deciles, then compares how much of the new data falls into each of those same bins.

body.caption: For each bin i, Expected% is the training data's share and Actual% is the new data's share of that same bin. A PSI near zero means the new data's shape closely matches training; a large PSI means the shape has genuinely moved.

cells: No significant shift; monitoring, no action needed
Significant shift; treat with real caution before trusting the agent's current behavior

body.code:
import numpy as np

def population_stability_index(reference, current, bins=10):
    reference, current = np.asarray(reference), np.asarray(current)
    breakpoints = np.percentile(reference, np.linspace(0, 100, bins + 1))
    breakpoints[0], breakpoints[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf

    ref_counts, _ = np.histogram(reference, bins=breakpoints)
    cur_counts, _ = np.histogram(current, bins=breakpoints)
    ref_pct = ref_counts / len(reference)
    cur_pct = cur_counts / len(current)

    epsilon = 1e-4  # avoids log(0) for empty bins
    ref_pct = np.where(ref_pct == 0, epsilon, ref_pct)
    cur_pct = np.where(cur_pct == 0, epsilon, cur_pct)

    return float(np.sum((cur_pct - ref_pct) * np.log(cur_pct / ref_pct)))
body.caption: Verified against three cases: comparing a distribution to a fresh sample of itself gave PSI = 0.011, well under the 0.10 threshold. Shifting the mean by half a standard deviation gave PSI = 0.255, just past the significant-shift line. More than doubling the variance gave PSI = 0.837, clearly significant.

children.text: Novelty Detection: Flagging Individual Live States in Real Time

KS tests and PSI both compare batches of data, useful for a daily or weekly monitoring check, but too slow for catching a single extreme state the moment it happens live. A k-nearest-neighbors distance check addresses this: measure how far a new state sits from its closest neighbors in the training data, and flag it if that distance is unusually large relative to how training data points sit relative to each other.

body.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

# Normalize using TRAIN statistics only, per Chapter 3's look-ahead bias warning
train_mean, train_std = train_matrix.mean(axis=0), train_matrix.std(axis=0)
train_norm = (train_matrix - train_mean) / train_std

nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=10)
nn.fit(train_norm)

# Calibrate a threshold from the training data's own internal novelty scores
train_distances, _ = nn.kneighbors(train_norm)
threshold = np.percentile(train_distances.mean(axis=1), 99)

def novelty_score(state, mean=train_mean, std=train_std, model=nn):
    normalized = (np.asarray(state).reshape(1, -1) - mean) / std
    distances, _ = model.kneighbors(normalized)
    return distances.mean()
body.caption: The threshold is calibrated from the training data itself, the 99th percentile of how far a typical training point sits from its own nearest neighbors, so a live state is only flagged if it is meaningfully more isolated than almost anything the agent actually trained on.

children.text: What to Actually Do When Shift Is Detected

body.caption: Responses to a Detected Shift, and Their Tradeoffs

cells: Scale exposure down proportionally to the novelty score once it crosses a threshold
Keeps some participation, but requires a well-tested sizing rule of its own
Close existing positions and stop taking new ones until a human reviews the situation
Safest option, but means missing any genuine opportunity during the pause, and needs a human actually available to review
Log the flag and notify a human, but let the agent continue acting
Fastest, least disruptive, but only useful if the human alerted can act quickly enough to matter
Not a real option, included for contrast
This is the default behavior without any of this lesson's tooling, and it is exactly the failure mode Chapter 1 described

body.text: Every threshold in this lesson trades off two failure modes: too strict, and ordinary daily noise triggers false alarms often enough that a human stops trusting or checking them at all; too loose, and a genuine shift slips through. There is no universally correct setting; it needs calibrating against the specific strategy's own tolerance for missed alerts versus alarm fatigue, and revisited periodically, since a threshold calibrated once on old training data can itself grow stale as the strategy's normal operating range slowly changes.

body.title: Choosing a Response to a Borderline PSI Reading
body.scenario: A weekly PSI check on india_vix comes back at 0.16, inside the 0.10 to 0.25 moderate-shift range this lesson's threshold table describes, not clearly safe and not clearly severe. The same week's k-NN novelty checks on individual live states have not flagged anything.
body.prompt: Given both signals together, what response from this lesson's table would you choose, and why?
body.modelAnswer: A moderate PSI reading with no individual states flagged suggests a real but gradual shift in the overall distribution of india_vix, volatility drifting to a somewhat different range, rather than the sudden, extreme kind of event the k-NN check is specifically built to catch. This combination points toward the 'alert only, keep trading' response rather than an immediate flatten-and-pause: nothing in the live data has actually looked individually alarming, so there is no clear trigger for the most disruptive response, but a moderate PSI reading is exactly the kind of early signal that deserves human attention before it potentially develops into something the KS test or a novelty check would catch more severely later. Escalating straight to flatten-and-pause on a moderate PSI alone, with no corroborating individual-state signal, risks exactly the alarm-fatigue problem the closing warning described.

body.title: Why the k-NN Threshold Is Calibrated From Training Data
body.question: In this lesson's novelty detection code, the threshold is set using the 99th percentile of the training data's own internal nearest-neighbor distances, rather than an arbitrary fixed number. Why does this matter?
options: It doesn't matter; any fixed threshold would work identically

Calibrating from the training data's own internal distances sets a threshold relative to how spread out normal training states already are, so the flag only fires for states meaningfully more isolated than almost anything the agent actually learned from, rather than an arbitrary number disconnected from that specific state space
It is required by the Gymnasium interface
It only matters when using DQN, not PPO
body.explanation: Different state representations, feature scales, and strategies will naturally have different typical distances between their own training points. Calibrating the threshold from training data's own internal spread means the flag adapts to whatever the agent's actual training distribution looks like, rather than relying on an arbitrary fixed cutoff that might be meaningless for a differently scaled or structured state space.

points: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compares two samples' distributions feature by feature, producing a p-value that flags genuine shifts, verified here to correctly flag only a deliberately shifted feature (india_vix) while leaving unshifted features alone

Population Stability Index gives a single number per feature with standard thresholds (below 0.10 fine, 0.10 to 0.25 worth investigating, above 0.25 significant), verified against known shifted and unshifted cases

Both KS and PSI compare batches of data and suit periodic monitoring; a k-nearest-neighbors distance check complements them by flagging individual live states in real time, calibrated from the training data's own internal spread
The verified k-NN check correctly passed a normal live state (score 0.34, threshold 1.16) and correctly flagged a crash-like extreme state (score 18.47, roughly 16 times the threshold)

Detecting shift is only useful paired with a real response: reducing size, flattening and pausing, or alerting a human, matched to how severe and how corroborated the signal is, not silently continuing as if nothing changed

Every threshold in this lesson trades false alarms against missed shifts, and needs calibrating to the specific strategy's tolerance and periodic revisiting, since a threshold set once can itself grow stale
